title: On how natural and urban soundscapes alter brain activity during cognitive performance
research_question: To inquire the effect of listening to urban vs. natural soundscapes on cognitive performance, mood, stress reactivity, and brain activity during a subsequent cognitive task, assessed before and after soundscape exposure.

participants.description: 30 participants (12 female, 23 male, 0 non-binary, mean age = 27.6 years) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision, not taking psychotropic medications.
participants.recruitment: Participants were invited for three subsequent days to the Max Planck Institute for Human Development, Berlin, Germany. All participants provided informed consent and received monetary compensation.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 40 natural soundscapes (bird-songs, water, insects, wind) and 40 urban soundscapes (traffic, café ambiance, machinery noise). Each soundscape was 20s long with 500-ms linear fade in/out, total exposure 13.3 min. A 'no-soundscape' control condition was also used.
Backward Digit Span (BDS) task (computer and fMRI versions) and Dual N-Back (DNB) task (computer and fMRI versions).

measures.instrument: fMRI (Superior Temporal Gyrus, Medial Prefrontal Cortex, Inferior Parietal Lobule)

findings.antecedent: Natural soundscape exposure (decrease in negative affect)
findings.consequent: Inferior Parietal Lobule (IPL) activity during DNB task
findings.mechanism: A decrease in negative emotions is associated with less activity in the IPL, suggesting reduced cognitive control effort needed for task processing.
findings.quote: a decrease in negative emotions was associated with less activity in the IPL region during the dual n-back task following the exposure to natural soundscapes.

mechanisms: Attention Restoration Theory (ART): Natural environments minimize demands on voluntary/directed attention, allowing it to recharge.
Stress Recovery Theory (SRT): Affective and aesthetic values from nature lower stress levels, creating room for improved cognitive performance.
Neural efficiency: Restored attentional capacities lead to more effective or economical processing in task-relevant brain regions (e.g., less mPFC activity for better performance).

Reduced information processing load: Less negative affect is associated with reduced activity in cognitive control networks (IPL), suggesting less effort is needed to process task-related information.
implementation_implications: Knowledge gained should be used in future educational contexts to train children to increase attention, potentially through repeated outdoor exploration sessions or playing nature sounds gently in classrooms.
Tailored interventions should aim to maximize nature's benefits or minimize negative urban effects.
limitations: Numerically higher number of male participants (23 males vs 12 females) due to recruitment challenges.
Difficulty in justifying a 'neutral' sound condition, as MRI scanner noise was present and perceived differently by participants.
Usage of difference scores (post-pre) for correlations, which showed low reliability for fMRI-adjusted scan tasks.
Exhaustive task procedure potentially resulting in confounding effects of learning.
Long delay between the scanner intervention and the post-test computer tasks, making interpretation of computer task behavioral results difficult.
The main fMRI result (STG activity) was uncorrected for multiple comparisons and remains exploratory.
The cognitive effect did not reach significance in the main analysis.
